blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A budget of 10 and three items, already in ratio order: A costs 4 and is worth 12, B costs 5 and is worth 10, C costs 3 and is worth 3. What is Dantzig's bound?

options.text: 22: A and B whole, and C left out since it does not fit
options.says: That is a real plan, not the LP: the LP takes the fraction of C that the last 1 of budget buys.

options.text: 25: all three items whole, since the bound may break the budget
options.says: The LP keeps the budget row; it relaxes only the 0-1 rule, so C can be taken only in part.

options.text: 24: A whole and the 6 left spent on B at its ratio of 2
options.says: B costs 5 and fits whole, leaving 1; the fill takes items whole while they fit, then a fraction of the next.

options.text: 23: A and B whole, and one third of C with the 1 left over
options.says: Right: 12 + 10 for A and B (cost 9), then 1/3 of C for 1, worth 3 x 1/3 = 1.

origin.section: A One-Row LP Is Solved by Sorting: Dantzig's Bound

questions.stem: The free items, in ratio order, are P, Q and R. A node of the knapsack search fixes Q at 1 and P at 0. How is that node's LP value found?

options.text: Re-sort the free items by ratio, then fill from the start as at the root
options.says: Fixings change neither value nor cost, so the free items keep their order; one sort serves every node.

options.text: Apply the fixings to the budget first, then fill the rest in ratio order
options.says: Right: items fixed at 1 are paid first whatever their ratio, items fixed at 0 are skipped, the rest fill in order.

options.text: Hand the node to an LP solver, since fixings break the ratio order
options.says: The fill still is the LP with fixings; the lesson's GLOP check matched it at the split item's children.

options.text: Fill every item in ratio order, then swap values to match the fixings
options.says: P is fixed at 0 and never taken; Q is paid for first, before any free item.

origin.section: Fixing an Item Changes the Budget, Not the Order

questions.stem: On the tiny portfolio the knapsack search returns a plan worth 3,892 with must-dos, which funds both P006 and P007, two alternatives. The full selection model's best is 3,627. Why the difference?

options.text: Only the budget row is kept, so nothing stops two rival projects together
options.says: Right: the knapsack drops the parent and alternative rows, a relaxation, so its optimum can be higher and its plan can break them.

options.text: Dantzig's bound runs looser than GLOP's, so the search overshoots
options.says: Dantzig's bound equals the LP relaxation; the program checked it against GLOP to the last digit printed.

options.text: The search stopped at a fractional node and rounded its value up
options.says: The search only records integral nodes as plans; 3,892 is a whole plan of the knapsack model.

options.text: The must-do value is counted twice, once in the budget and once in the plan
options.says: The must-do is paid for once, before the search, and its value 871 is added once: 3,021 + 871.
